claims.claim: QDiabetes-2018 used Cox models and baseline predictors to estimate ten-year incident T2D risk, with non-glycaemic, FPG and HbA1c model variants.

location.section: Derivation and validation of the models

claims.claim: QDiabetes-2018 assessed calibration and decision curves; its validation practices remained within QResearch, and the authors requested independent external validation.

location.section: Validation of the models; Decision curve analysis; Discussion

claims.claim: Sasagawa compared seven-year DeepSurv and Cox models using a stratified random split of the same J-ECOH cohort.
For diabetes, AUROC was 0.878 for DeepSurv and 0.872 for Cox. Discussion states AUROC/Brier differences were not significant, although NRI/IDI improved.
The Sasagawa outcome did not distinguish type 2, type 1 or gestational diabetes; public deposition of data had ethical/legal restrictions.

Xu externally validated published risk models in three Chinese intermediate-hyperglycemia cohorts, finding nonuniform discrimination and poor calibration of models with sufficient risk-equation information.

location.section: Results / External validation of the included models

claims.claim: Xu rescaled risk estimates across differing prediction horizons using an assumed constant annual diabetes-progression risk.

location.section: Methods / paragraph immediately before Discrimination and calibration

claims.claim: The JPHC study used logistic regression for five-year incident diabetes prediction, developed in JPHC and validated in J-ECOH, comparing non-invasive and glycaemic-predictor models.
Lugner studied ten-year T2D incidence using UK Biobank baseline data and XGBoost, with an 80/20 within-cohort train/validation split.
Lugner emphasized predictor prioritization as the study purpose and directed data applicants to the UK Biobank Access Management System.
Zhang compared seven algorithms for five-year progression in baseline prediabetes patients from two Chinese centers, including a separate-center external cohort.
Zhang required baseline HbA1c 5.7-6.4%, assessed progression at HbA1c >=6.5%, and stated data availability on reasonable request.
Kiviniemi used clinically incident T2D from registers, primarily at five years, developing in one Finnish cohort and externally validating in four others.

location.section: 2.1 Overall study design; 2.3 Outcome and predictor variables

claims.claim: Kiviniemi reported limited added predictive value of metabolic measures over clinical baseline and poor calibration generalization; authors lacked permission to share data.
Huang developed baseline clinical Cox models after LASSO-Cox, random-survival-forest and best-subset variable selection in Whitehall II, externally validated in ELSA for 5-, 10- and 15-year risk.
Huang acknowledged ELSA self-reported diabetes, possible model-selection optimism, complete-case selection and absence of competing-risk analysis.

uncertainty: No systematic completeness, formal study-quality audit or exhaustive integrity check is claimed.
All eight have evidence value for framing; none is certified as a reproduction candidate because present data access and complete implementation feasibility were not established.
No novel algorithm, dataset, five-year horizon, hypothesis or clinical-use claim is frozen.
Need a feasible longitudinal dataset with a verified incident-T2D endpoint, baseline eligibility, follow-up/censoring and predictor timing before deciding the actual contribution.
General diabetes-free populations and prediabetes cohorts must not be pooled as an identical prediction target.
Sasagawa is a survival-method reference, with broader diabetes outcome; mortality/complications, current diagnosis, CGM and genomic-only work are not substitute evidence for the target.
Calibration, independent evaluation and fair clinical baseline comparison are possible manageable evaluation priorities, not proven local literature gaps or mandatory upgrades.
Repeated-history and missing-HbA1c extensions remain parked; literature does not make them obligatory.
